On the Reliability Limits of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Planning

Ruicheng Ao    Siyang Gao    David Simchi-Levi
August 24, 2026
Abstract

This technical note studies the reliability limits of LLM-based multi-agent planning as a delegated decision problem. We model the LLM-based multi-agent architecture as a finite acyclic decision network in which multiple stages process shared model-context information, communicate through language interfaces with limited capacity, and may invoke human review. We show that, without new exogenous signals, any delegated network is decision-theoretically dominated by a centralized Bayes decision maker with access to the same information. In the common-evidence regime, this implies that optimizing over multi-agent directed acyclic graphs under a finite communication budget can be recast as choosing a budget-constrained stochastic experiment on the shared signal. We also characterize the loss induced by communication and information compression. Under proper scoring rules, the gap between the centralized Bayes value and the value after communication admits an expected posterior divergence representation, which reduces to conditional mutual information under logarithmic loss and to expected squared posterior error under the Brier score. These results characterize the fundamental reliability limits of delegated LLM planning. Experiments with LLMs on a controlled problem set further demonstrate these characterizations.

Keywords: LLM agents, decision theory, information structure, delegated decisions

1 Introduction

LLM-based multi-agent planning is now widely used for operational tasks that require decomposition, tool use, verification, and exception handling, such as customer service handling, document-based analysis, scheduling and coordination, and web-based task execution. From an operations research perspective, these systems can be naturally viewed as delegated decision networks, where different stages process shared model-context information, communicate through language interfaces with limited capacity, and may invoke human review. In this setting, the key design question is not how many roles the system contains, but whether the added roles change the information structure, where here the information structure means what decision-relevant signals enter the system and what part of those signals is still available when the terminal action is chosen.

This distinction is central in current LLM-based agent systems because many architectures add roles without adding new decision-relevant signals. Planner, worker, critic, and reviewer modules are often built from the same model family, operate on overlapping retrieved context, and communicate through free-form language. In such cases, the added stages mainly transform and relay shared evidence rather than expand the information available for the terminal decision.

Recent empirical work is consistent with this concern. Performance on web-interaction, assistant, and computer-use tasks often remains fragile as tasks involve more steps, more tool use, and more coordination (Liu et al. 2023, Zhou et al. 2024, Mialon et al. 2024, Xie et al. 2024). Reported failures frequently arise from specification and coordination rather than from base-model capability (Cemri et al. 2025), and simpler single-agent designs can match multi-agent performance at lower cost while longer multi-step systems may amplify the errors (Xia et al. 2024, Kim et al. 2025, Wan et al. 2025, Wynn et al. 2025).

At the same time, recent developments on LLM agents suggest which changes may help. Reasoning models can improve performance by investing more inference-time computation on the same evidence, while protocols on tool use help when they introduce genuinely new exogenous signals rather than merely reprocessing shared context (Wan et al. 2025, Xu et al. 2026). These observations point to a common mechanism that architecture matters through the information made available for the terminal decision.

This note provides a decision-theoretic account of this mechanism by modeling an LLM-based agent system as a finite acyclic delegated decision network.

First, we show a basic limit that, without new exogenous signals, a delegated network cannot outperform a centralized Bayes decision maker that observes the same information. In the common-evidence regime, optimizing over multi-agent directed acyclic graphs under a finite communication budget is equivalent to choosing how to compress and pass along the shared signal.

Second, we characterize the cost of communication and the role of human review. Under proper scoring rules, the gap between the centralized Bayes value and the value after communication is exactly the loss from posterior distortion. Under logarithmic loss, this becomes conditional mutual information, and under the Brier score, it becomes expected squared posterior error. Human review should therefore focus on cases with high posterior risk.

Third, we test these ideas on a controlled problem set using recent LLMs, and find qualitative patterns consistent with the theory.

The main contribution of this research is to identify what kind of design can actually improve the reliability of LLM-based agent systems. Added stages help only when they bring in new exogenous signals, preserve decision-relevant information under communication constraints, or provide non-redundant review. Otherwise, they mainly reorganize the same evidence. In this note, we use the term reliability in an operational sense, namely as the quality of the terminal decision under a specified loss function. In the analysis, this is represented by Bayes risk or expected loss.

Related work.

This research builds on the team decision theory (Radner 1962, Marschak and Radner 1972, Ho and Chu 1972), which studies decentralized decision making under shared and private information, and on the Blackwell comparison of experiments (Blackwell 1953, Torgersen 1991), which formalizes when one information structure is more informative than another. Our analysis of communication loss uses proper scoring rules (Gneiting and Raftery 2007), and our result on selective review relates to reject-option classification (Chow 1970, El-Yaniv and Wiener 2010). More broadly, the operations research literature on prescriptive analytics studies how information quality affects decision quality (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020, Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022, Bastani 2021), and our framework applies the same principle to LLM-based multi-agent workflows, where the information is the terminal communication state and the decision is the final action. On the LLM side, recent work reports failure modes in multi-agent systems (Cemri et al. 2025, Wan et al. 2025, Huang et al. 2024, Kim et al. 2025) and compares them with simpler single agent alternatives (Xia et al. 2024, Xu et al. 2026).

The starting point of this research differs from the studies mentioned above. We do not aim to propose a new multi-agent workflow or to add one more empirical comparison among agentic variants, but rather to develop a minimal decision-theoretic model in which alternative LLM-based multi-agent workflows can be compared through the information available for the final choice, the communication constraints imposed between stages, and the availability of selective review. This model is useful for operations research because it recasts workflow design as a stochastic problem of information, communication, and costly recourse, rather than as a taxonomy of software roles.

2 Delegated Decision Model

An LLM-based agent system usually operates through a simple workflow. A user request or task instance first provides the shared context for the system. The task is then processed through several stages, such as planning, tool use, execution, verification, and final decision making. Different agents or modules may handle different stages, exchange intermediate messages, and in some cases call external tools or escalate difficult cases for human review.

We model such a system as a finite directed acyclic graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E). This abstraction is natural because it represents each stage as a decision node and each communication link as an edge that carries information to later stages. It captures the aspects of agent-based systems that matter for reliability (specifically, the information that is entered, communicated, and available for the terminal action). A hidden task state X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} determines the relevant facts, constraints, and environment conditions. Let YY denote the target of interest, such as the correct action or label. The network does not observe XX or YY directly. Instead, it acts on the basis of signals generated from the task state.

The system may observe a common signal BB, drawn from a kernel K0(⋅∣X)K_{0}(\cdot\mid X). This signal represents the shared model-context information available to the network, such as the user request, retrieved documents, task instructions, or a common workspace. Node vv may also observe a private exogenous signal ZvZ_{v}, drawn from a kernel Kv(⋅∣X)K_{v}(\cdot\mid X). These private signals represent new information that enters at a particular stage, such as a tool output, a database lookup, executable feedback, or an environment observation. We write Z𝒱:={Zv:v∈V}Z_{\mathcal{V}}:=\{Z_{v}:v\in V\} and Eexo:=(B,Z𝒱)E^{\mathrm{exo}}:=(B,Z_{\mathcal{V}}), where the object EexoE^{\mathrm{exo}} is the total exogenous information available to the delegated system. Each edge e=(u,v)∈Ee=(u,v)\in E carries a message from node uu to node vv. Let UuU_{u} denote the upstream workspace at node uu. The message sent on edge ee is Te=Tu→v=σe​(Uu,ξe)T_{e}=T_{u\to v}=\sigma_{e}(U_{u},\xi_{e}), where σe\sigma_{e} is a measurable communication rule and ξe\xi_{e} is ancillary randomization. Node vv then acts according to a measurable decision rule Av=πv​(Hv,ξv)A_{v}=\pi_{v}(H_{v},\xi_{v}), where HvH_{v} collects incoming messages together with any exogenous signals observed at node vv. Let ξ\xi collect all ancillary randomness and assume that ξ\xi is independent of Y|EexoY\mid E^{\mathrm{exo}}. Since the graph is acyclic, the full protocol induces a measurable terminal action A=Π⁡(G,Eexo,ξ)A=\Pi(G,E^{\mathrm{exo}},\xi).

Note that this formulation works at the level of information structure rather than token-level generation. This level is the one most relevant for the reliability.

For a loss function ℓ:𝒜×𝒴→[0,∞]\ell:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[0,\infty], we define the Bayes risk under information state HH by

V⁡(H,ℓ):=infδ∈𝒟⁡(H)𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(δ⁡(H),Y)],V(H;\ell):=\inf_{\delta\in\mathcal{D}(H)}\mathbb{E}[\ell(\delta(H),Y)],

which we use as a decision-theoretic measure of reliability. Here 𝒟⁡(H)\mathcal{D}(H) denotes the class of decision rules measurable with respect to the universal completion of σ⁡(H)\sigma(H). This is the standard convention in stochastic control on standard Borel spaces. It ensures the existence of ε\varepsilon-optimal decision rules and does not affect the finite-action cases used later.

An important special case for our analysis is the common-evidence regime, defined by Zv≡∅Z_{v}\equiv\varnothing for all v∈Vv\in V. In this case, Eexo=BE^{\mathrm{exo}}=B, so all nodes process the same underlying evidence. This regime is not only analytically convenient. It is also common in practice and is especially relevant for planner, worker, critic, and reviewer architectures that share the same prompt, retrieval context, or message history. In such settings, added roles often do not bring new decision-relevant signals. They mainly reprocess shared evidence and pass along a compressed version of it.

When communication limits matter, we summarize what reaches the final decision stage by a terminal communication state MM. This object may be a transcript, a structured state record, or any equivalent bundle of information. Any object visible to the terminal decision can be folded into MM. We also allow a review option at the final stage. In that case, the action set is augmented by △\triangle, where △\triangle denotes escalate. Review incurs conditional loss Rh​(H)R_{h}(H), which may depend on the information state through review cost, delay, or reviewer quality.

All probability spaces, state spaces, action spaces, and signal spaces are assumed to be standard Borel, and all kernels are measurable. Table 1 summarizes the abstract variables in our delegated decision network and the corresponding components of LLM-based multi-agent planning (shared context, stage-specific inputs, inter-agent communication, and the final information available for the terminal decision). It clarifies how the abstract objects in our model map to a typical LLM-based multi-agent workflow.

3 Preliminaries

This section provides several basic lemmas that support the analysis in the next sections. Throughout the note, when we say that a rule is HH-measurable, we mean measurable with respect to the universal completion of σ⁡(H)\sigma(H). We only need ε\varepsilon-optimal attainment unless exact attainment is stated explicitly. On standard Borel spaces, regular conditional distributions, lower semianalytic value functions, and universally measurable ε\varepsilon-optimal selectors are available by standard results. See, for example, Bertsekas and Shreve (1978) and Kallenberg (2002). When the action space is finite, this distinction from ordinary Borel measurability disappears. We adopt this convention only to avoid compactness or continuity assumptions that are not needed for the finite-message and finite-action applications in the paper.

Lemma 1.

Let HH be any information state and let ℓ:𝒜×𝒴→ℝ+\ell:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} be bounded. Define Λ⁡(h,a):=𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(a,Y)∣H=h]\Lambda(h,a):=\mathbb{E}[\ell(a,Y)\mid H=h]. Then the Bayes risk V⁡(H,ℓ)V(H;\ell) satisfies

V⁡(H,ℓ)=𝔼⁡[infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)].V(H;\ell)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)\right].

Moreover, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists an HH-measurable selector δε\delta_{\varepsilon} such that Λ⁡(H,δε​(H))≤infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)+ε\Lambda(H,\delta_{\varepsilon}(H))\leq\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)+\varepsilon almost surely, and therefore 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(δε​(H),Y)]≤V⁡(H,ℓ)+ε\mathbb{E}[\ell(\delta_{\varepsilon}(H),Y)]\leq V(H;\ell)+\varepsilon.

Proof. Let νh(⋅):=ℙ(Y∈⋅∣H=h)\nu_{h}(\cdot):=\mathbb{P}(Y\in\cdot\mid H=h) be a regular conditional distribution of YY given HH. Then

Λ⁡(h,a)=∫𝒴ℓ⁡(a,y)​νh​(𝑑y),\Lambda(h,a)=\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\ell(a,y)\,\nu_{h}(dy),

which is jointly measurable in (h,a)(h,a) because ℓ\ell is measurable and h↦νhh\mapsto\nu_{h} is a kernel. The value function v⁡(h):=infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(h,a)v(h):=\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(h,a) is lower semianalytic, and thus universally measurable. For any HH-measurable rule δ\delta,

𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(δ⁡(H),Y)∣H]=Λ⁡(H,δ⁡(H))≥infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)a.s.\mathbb{E}[\ell(\delta(H),Y)\mid H]=\Lambda(H,\delta(H))\geq\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)\qquad\text{a.s.}

Taking expectations and infimizing over all HH-measurable δ\delta gives V⁡(H,ℓ)≥𝔼⁡[infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)]V(H;\ell)\geq\mathbb{E}[\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)].

Conversely, by a standard measurable-selection theorem for lower semianalytic costs on standard Borel spaces (Bertsekas and Shreve 1978), for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists an HH-measurable selector δε\delta_{\varepsilon} satisfying

Λ⁡(H,δε​(H))≤infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)+εa.s.\Lambda(H,\delta_{\varepsilon}(H))\leq\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)+\varepsilon\qquad\text{a.s.}

Taking expectations gives 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(δε​(H),Y)]≤𝔼⁡[infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)]+ε\mathbb{E}[\ell(\delta_{\varepsilon}(H),Y)]\leq\mathbb{E}[\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)]+\varepsilon. Since ε>0\varepsilon>0 is arbitrary, V⁡(H,ℓ)≤𝔼⁡[infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)]V(H;\ell)\leq\mathbb{E}[\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)]. □\square

Lemma 1 gives a convenient representation of the best achievable loss under a given information state. It will be used when we replace a terminal decision rule by a Bayes-optimal one and when we need an ε\varepsilon-optimal measurable selector (Proposition 6, Theorem 7, and Theorem 10).

Lemma 2.

Let HH be any information state, Γ(⋅∣H)\Gamma(\cdot\mid H) be an HH-measurable kernel on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and AΓA_{\Gamma} be an action drawn from Γ(⋅∣H)\Gamma(\cdot\mid H) such that ℙ⁡(AΓ∈C∣H,Y)=Γ⁡(C∣H)\mathbb{P}(A_{\Gamma}\in C\mid H,Y)=\Gamma(C\mid H) a.s. for every Borel set C⊆𝒜C\subseteq\mathcal{A}. Then 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(AΓ,Y)]≥V⁡(H,ℓ)\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\Gamma},Y)]\geq V(H;\ell). Consequently, if MM is generated from HH by a kernel that is independent of YY conditional on HH, then V⁡(M,ℓ)≥V⁡(H,ℓ)V(M;\ell)\geq V(H;\ell).

Proof. Let Λ\Lambda be as in Lemma 1. Conditional on HH, 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(AΓ,Y)∣H]=∫𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)​Γ​(𝑑a∣H)≥infa∈𝒜Λ⁡(H,a)\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\Gamma},Y)\mid H]=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a)\,\Gamma(da\mid H)\geq\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Lambda(H,a) a.s. Taking expectations and applying Lemma 1 gives 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(AΓ,Y)]≥V⁡(H,ℓ)\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\Gamma},Y)]\geq V(H;\ell).

For the second claim, fix any MM-measurable rule δ⁡(M)\delta(M). Since MM is generated from HH through a kernel that is conditionally independent of YY, the random action δ⁡(M)\delta(M) satisfies ℙ⁡(δ⁡(M)∈C∣H,Y)=ℙ⁡(δ⁡(M)∈C∣H)\mathbb{P}(\delta(M)\in C\mid H,Y)=\mathbb{P}(\delta(M)\in C\mid H) a.s. for every Borel C⊆𝒜C\subseteq\mathcal{A}. Applying the first part with AΓ=δ⁡(M)A_{\Gamma}=\delta(M) and infimizing over MM-measurable δ\delta gives V⁡(M,ℓ)≥V⁡(H,ℓ)V(M;\ell)\geq V(H;\ell). □\square

Lemma 2 states that once information is compressed through a conditionally independent channel, decision quality cannot improve. This is the basic comparison step behind the later results on delegated networks and communication (Proposition 6, Theorem 7, and Lemma 4).

Lemma 3.

Assume 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is finite. Let M=μ⁡(H,ζ)M=\mu(H,\zeta), where ζ⟂⟂Y|H\zeta\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid H, and define πH​(y):=ℙ⁡(Y=y∣H)\pi_{H}(y):=\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid H), πM​(y):=ℙ⁡(Y=y∣M)\pi_{M}(y):=\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid M). Then, for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, ℙ⁡(Y=y∣H,M)=πH​(y)\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid H,M)=\pi_{H}(y) a.s. and πM​(y)=𝔼⁡[πH​(y)∣M]\pi_{M}(y)=\mathbb{E}[\pi_{H}(y)\mid M] a.s.

Proof. Fix y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. Let f⁡(H,M)f(H,M) be any bounded measurable function. Since MM is measurable with respect to (H,ζ)(H,\zeta) and ζ⟂⟂Y|H\zeta\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid H,

𝔼[𝟏{Y=y}f(H,M)∣H]=πH(y)𝔼[f(H,M)∣H].\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{Y=y\}f(H,M)\mid H]=\pi_{H}(y)\mathbb{E}[f(H,M)\mid H].

Taking expectations gives 𝔼[𝟏{Y=y}f(H,M)]=𝔼[πH(y)f(H,M)]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{Y=y\}f(H,M)]=\mathbb{E}[\pi_{H}(y)f(H,M)]. Since this holds for every bounded measurable f⁡(H,M)f(H,M), the characterizing property of conditional expectation gives ℙ⁡(Y=y∣H,M)=πH​(y)\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid H,M)=\pi_{H}(y) a.s. Conditioning on MM and using the tower property, πM​(y)=𝔼⁡[ℙ⁡(Y=y∣H,M)∣M]=𝔼⁡[πH​(y)∣M]\pi_{M}(y)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid H,M)\mid M]=\mathbb{E}[\pi_{H}(y)\mid M]. □\square

Lemma 3 describes how the posterior changes after communication. It is the main posterior identity used to express communication loss as posterior distortion (Theorem 8).

Lemma 4.

Let SS and TT be two information states about YY, both taking values in standard Borel spaces.

  1. (a)

    If SS is generated from TT through a conditionally independent kernel, then V⁡(S,ℓ)≥V⁡(T,ℓ)V(S;\ell)\geq V(T;\ell) for every bounded loss ℓ\ell.

  2. (b)

    If SS is not Blackwell-dominated by TT, then there exist a finite action set 𝒜~\tilde{\mathcal{A}} and a bounded loss ℓ~:𝒜~×𝒴→ℝ\tilde{\ell}:\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} such that V⁡(S,ℓ~)<V⁡(T,ℓ~)V(S;\tilde{\ell})<V(T;\tilde{\ell}).

Proof. Part (a) is immediate from Lemma 2 with H=TH=T and M=SM=S. For part (b), Blackwell’s theorem on experiment comparison (Blackwell 1953, Torgersen 1991) implies that if SS is not Blackwell-dominated by TT, then there exist a finite action set 𝒜~\tilde{\mathcal{A}} and a bounded utility function u:𝒜~×𝒴→ℝu:\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} with strict expected-utility separation. Setting ℓ~​(a,y):=C−u⁡(a,y)\tilde{\ell}(a,y):=C-u(a,y) for C>supa,yu⁡(a,y)C>\sup_{a,y}u(a,y) converts the utility gap to V⁡(S,ℓ~)<V⁡(T,ℓ~)V(S;\tilde{\ell})<V(T;\tilde{\ell}). □\square

Lemma 4 gives the comparison result that we use to distinguish redundant signals from signals that can improve the decision problem. This lemma is used when we discuss verification gain and new exogenous information (Corollary 9).

Write ρ⁡(H):=Γ⁡({△}∣H)\rho(H):=\Gamma(\{\triangle\}\mid H) and α(⋅∣H):=Γ(⋅∩𝒜∣H)\alpha(\cdot\mid H):=\Gamma(\cdot\cap\mathcal{A}\mid H). Then ρ⁡(H)+α⁡(𝒜∣H)=1\rho(H)+\alpha(\mathcal{A}\mid H)=1 a.s., and

𝔼⁡[loss∣H]=∫𝒜𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(a,Y)∣H]​α​(𝑑a∣H)+ρ⁡(H)​Rh​(H)≥min⁡{Ra​(H),Rh​(H)},\mathbb{E}[\text{loss}\mid H]=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(a,Y)\mid H]\,\alpha(da\mid H)+\rho(H)R_{h}(H)\geq\min\{R_{a}(H),R_{h}(H)\},

because 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(a,Y)∣H]≥Ra​(H)\mathbb{E}[\ell(a,Y)\mid H]\geq R_{a}(H) for every aa and the coefficients are nonnegative and sum to 11. Taking expectations leads to the lower bound.

For the upper bound, fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. By Lemma 1, there exists an HH-measurable selector aε​(H)a_{\varepsilon}(H) with 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(aε​(H),Y)∣H]≤Ra​(H)+ε\mathbb{E}[\ell(a_{\varepsilon}(H),Y)\mid H]\leq R_{a}(H)+\varepsilon a.s. Use aε​(H)a_{\varepsilon}(H) on {Ra(H)≤Rh(H)}\{R_{a}(H)\leq R_{h}(H)\} and escalate otherwise. The resulting conditional loss satisfies 𝔼⁡[lossε∣H]≤min⁡{Ra​(H),Rh​(H)}+ε\mathbb{E}[\text{loss}_{\varepsilon}\mid H]\leq\min\{R_{a}(H),R_{h}(H)\}+\varepsilon. Taking expectations gives the claim. If Ra​(H)R_{a}(H) is attained by a∗​(H)a^{*}(H), taking aε=a∗a_{\varepsilon}=a^{*} gives an exact optimizer. □\square

Lemma 5 gives the basic rule for human review. The optimal decision compares automated posterior risk with review loss at each information state. This lemma is used to characterize the optimal selective review (Theorem 10).

4 Information Structure and Communication

This section examines the role of information structure in LLM-based multi-agent planning, focusing on what an architecture can change in the underlying decision problem. We begin with a general limit, where Proposition 6 shows that delegation alone does not improve the decision problem. We then turn to the common-evidence regime, with Theorem 7 showing that in this case, the design problem can be stated in a simpler form. This result also sets up the later sections, where we study the cost of communication and the value of added signals or human review.

Proposition 6.

Consider any finite directed acyclic delegated network G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with exogenous signals Eexo=(B,Z𝒱)E^{\mathrm{exo}}=(B,Z_{\mathcal{V}}), endogenous internal messages, and ancillary randomization ξ\xi satisfying ξ⟂⟂Y|Eexo\xi\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid E^{\mathrm{exo}}. Then for every bounded loss ℓ\ell11 1 Boundedness is assumed for simplicity. The results extend to integrable losses by standard approximation arguments.,

𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(A,Y)]≥V⁡(Eexo,ℓ).\mathbb{E}[\ell(A,Y)]\;\geq\;V(E^{\mathrm{exo}};\ell).

Equivalently, the delegated network is decision-theoretically dominated by a centralized Bayes decision maker observing the same exogenous signals EexoE^{\mathrm{exo}}.

Proof. Let E:=EexoE:=E^{\mathrm{exo}}. Since GG is acyclic, the delegated protocol induces a measurable terminal action A=Π⁡(G,E,ξ)A=\Pi(G,E,\xi). The key observation is that AA depends on YY only through EE. Since ξ⟂⟂Y|E\xi\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid E, the conditional law of AA given EE does not involve YY. In the language of Lemma 2, AA is a randomized garbling of EE, so

𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(A,Y)]≥V⁡(E,ℓ).\mathbb{E}[\ell(A,Y)]\geq V(E;\ell).

Thus internal communication and ancillary randomization cannot improve on the Bayes value determined by EE. □\square

Proposition 6 identifies the basic ceiling for delegated planning under fixed exogenous information, stating that neither internal communication nor randomization can improve upon the Bayes value of the available signals.

We now focus on the common-evidence regime, in which all nodes act on the same underlying signal and no stage receives new exogenous information. This case is both practically relevant for many LLM multi-agent workflows and conceptually useful, because it separates the effect of communication from that of signal acquisition.

Theorem 7.

Work in the standard Borel setting of Section 2 and in the common-evidence regime Eexo=BE^{\mathrm{exo}}=B. For a common-evidence information structure 𝒢\mathcal{G}, let A𝒢A_{\mathcal{G}} denote its terminal action and let M𝒢∈ℳ𝒢M_{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}} denote the finite terminal communication state delivered to the output stage. Define the communication budget C⁡(𝒢):=log⁡|ℳ𝒢|C(\mathcal{G}):=\log|\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}}|. Here the budget is the cardinality budget of the terminal communication state observed by the output stage. Let ℐC\mathcal{I}_{C} be the class of common-evidence information structures with C⁡(𝒢)≤CC(\mathcal{G})\leq C. Then for every bounded loss ℓ\ell,

inf𝒢∈ℐC𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(A𝒢,Y)]=infℳ finite,M∼Q(⋅∣B)log⁡|ℳ|≤CV⁡(M,ℓ),\inf_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{I}_{C}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\mathcal{G}},Y)]=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{M}\text{ finite},\,M\sim Q(\cdot\mid B)\\ \log|\mathcal{M}|\leq C\end{subarray}}V(M;\ell),

where the infimum on the right is over all stochastic encoders QQ from BB to a finite message MM.

Proof. To prove the equality stated in the theorem, we establish matching lower and upper bounds.

For the lower bound, fix 𝒢∈ℐC\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{I}_{C}. By the definition of the terminal state, the output stage observes only M𝒢M_{\mathcal{G}} and then chooses the terminal action through some M𝒢M_{\mathcal{G}}-measurable kernel. Replacing this output rule by a Bayes-optimal decision rule based on M𝒢M_{\mathcal{G}} can only improve performance, so Lemma 2 gives

𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(A𝒢,Y)]≥V⁡(M𝒢,ℓ).\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\mathcal{G}},Y)]\geq V(M_{\mathcal{G}};\ell).

Since we are in the common-evidence regime, the terminal communication state M𝒢M_{\mathcal{G}} is generated from the common signal BB together with ancillary randomization. Therefore its conditional law given BB, Q𝒢(⋅∣B):=ℙ(M𝒢∈⋅∣B)Q_{\mathcal{G}}(\cdot\mid B):=\mathbb{P}(M_{\mathcal{G}}\in\cdot\mid B), defines a stochastic encoder from BB to the finite message space ℳ𝒢\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}}. By construction, log⁡|ℳ𝒢|≤C\log|\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}}|\leq C. Therefore every 𝒢∈ℐC\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{I}_{C} induces an admissible encoder on the right-hand side, and

inf𝒢∈ℐC𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(A𝒢,Y)]≥infℳ finite,M∼Q(⋅∣B)log⁡|ℳ|≤CV⁡(M,ℓ).\inf_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{I}_{C}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\mathcal{G}},Y)]\geq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{M}\text{ finite},\,M\sim Q(\cdot\mid B)\\ \log|\mathcal{M}|\leq C\end{subarray}}V(M;\ell).

For the upper bound, fix any finite-valued encoder Q(⋅∣B)Q(\cdot\mid B) with log⁡|ℳ|≤C\log|\mathcal{M}|\leq C and any ε>0\varepsilon>0. Construct a two-stage common-evidence information structure. An encoder node samples M∼Q(⋅∣B)M\sim Q(\cdot\mid B). An output node applies an MM-measurable ε\varepsilon-optimal selector δε\delta_{\varepsilon} satisfying 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(δε​(M),Y)]≤V⁡(M,ℓ)+ε\mathbb{E}[\ell(\delta_{\varepsilon}(M),Y)]\leq V(M;\ell)+\varepsilon by Lemma 1. This information structure belongs to ℐC\mathcal{I}_{C}, so

inf𝒢∈ℐC𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(A𝒢,Y)]≤V⁡(M,ℓ)+ε.\inf_{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{I}_{C}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(A_{\mathcal{G}},Y)]\leq V(M;\ell)+\varepsilon.

Taking the infimum over admissible encoders QQ and then letting ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 proves the reverse inequality. □\square

Theorem 7 shows that, in the common-evidence regime, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph is decision-theoretically equivalent to the finite experiment Q⁡(m∣B)Q(m\mid B) that it induces on the shared signal. At a fixed budget, any loss from delegation therefore comes from acting on MM rather than on the original signal BB.

Remark 1.

Theorem 7 places the common-evidence design problem within familiar decision-theoretic frameworks. Choosing the encoder Q⁡(m∣B)Q(m\mid B) to minimize expected loss at a given budget is a Bayesian persuasion problem (Kamenica and Gentzkow 2011) in which the information structure selects what the output stage will observe. The same problem can be formulated as a rational inattention problem (Sims 2003) when the budget is measured by Shannon mutual information, and as an information bottleneck problem (Tishby et al. 2000) when relevance is measured by I⁡(M,Y)I(M;Y). In decentralized settings with genuinely private signals, Witsenhausen’s counterexample shows that optimal rules can require implicit signaling through actions (Witsenhausen 1968). This is why our reduction is specific to the common-evidence regime. The contribution here is to show that LLM-based multi-agent planning in the common-evidence regime fits exactly into this class of signal design problems. When agents instead observe genuinely different private signals, the problem returns to a nontrivial team decision setting and the reduction no longer applies.

Remark 2.

At a fixed budget, suppose a structured interface MsM_{s} Blackwell-dominates a free-text relay MtM_{t} for the target YY. Then any information structure that uses MtM_{t} is weakly dominated by one that uses MsM_{s}. The relevant design object is not the role label but the experiment induced by the communication interface.

Remark 3.

Theorem 7 has a useful methodological implication. In empirical evaluations of LLM agent architectures, improvements are often attributed to better coordination or better decomposition even when the compared systems differ simultaneously in tool access, retrieved context, or transcript length. Our result shows that such comparisons cannot distinguish a genuine architecture effect from a change in information. When exogenous information and terminal communication budget are not held fixed, any observed gain may reflect added information rather than improved delegation. Accordingly, a clean evaluation of multi-agent planning should compare architectures under matched exogenous signals and matched terminal state capacity, and should treat any additional retrieval, tool output, or larger shared workspace as a change in information structure rather than as a pure architecture effect. This also implies that many reported multi-agent gains should be interpreted as gains from altered information access unless the comparison explicitly controls for both exogenous signals and communication capacity.

5 Communication Loss and Posterior Distortion

In this section, we measure the loss from communication. Under proper scoring rules, the Bayes value depends only on the posterior. This allows us to write the gap between the centralized Bayes value and the value after communication as an expected posterior distortion. The next theorem gives this representation and yields the log-loss and Brier-score formulas stated below. In this section we assume that 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is finite, so that posteriors can be represented as elements of Δ⁡(𝒴)\Delta(\mathcal{Y}).

Theorem 8.

Let HH be any information state and let M=μ⁡(H,ζ)M=\mu(H,\zeta), where ζ\zeta is independent of Y|HY\mid H. Consider the action space to be the report space Δ⁡(𝒴)\Delta(\mathcal{Y}), so that a decision rule reports some q⁡(H)∈Δ⁡(𝒴)q(H)\in\Delta(\mathcal{Y}). Write πH:=ℙ(Y∈⋅∣H)\pi_{H}:=\mathbb{P}(Y\in\cdot\mid H) and πM:=ℙ(Y∈⋅∣M)\pi_{M}:=\mathbb{P}(Y\in\cdot\mid M). Let s:Δ⁡(𝒴)×𝒴→[0,∞]s:\Delta(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{Y}\to[0,\infty] be a proper scoring rule such that 𝔼⁡[s⁡(πH,Y)]\mathbb{E}[s(\pi_{H},Y)] and 𝔼⁡[s⁡(πM,Y)]\mathbb{E}[s(\pi_{M},Y)] are finite, and define its pointwise divergence by Ds​(p,q):=∑y∈𝒴p⁡(y)​(s⁡(q,y)−s⁡(p,y))D_{s}(p,q):=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p(y)\bigl(s(q,y)-s(p,y)\bigr). Then

V⁡(M,s)−V⁡(H,s)=𝔼⁡[Ds​(πH,πM)]≥0.V(M;s)-V(H;s)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[D_{s}(\pi_{H},\pi_{M})\bigr]\geq 0.

In particular, if H=BH=B and MM is the terminal communication state induced by a common-evidence information structure, then the left-hand side is exactly the gap between the centralized Bayes value and the value after communication. If ss is strictly proper, this gap is zero if and only if πH=πM\pi_{H}=\pi_{M} almost surely.

Proof. Here the decision problem is a reporting problem with action space Δ⁡(𝒴)\Delta(\mathcal{Y}). Since ss is proper, the Bayes-optimal report under any information state is the true posterior. Formally, for any admissible Δ⁡(𝒴)\Delta(\mathcal{Y})-valued report q⁡(H)q(H), propriety gives ∑yπH​(y)​s​(q⁡(H),y)≥∑yπH​(y)​s​(πH,y)\sum_{y}\pi_{H}(y)s(q(H),y)\geq\sum_{y}\pi_{H}(y)s(\pi_{H},y) pointwise. Conditioning on HH and taking expectations gives 𝔼⁡[s⁡(q⁡(H),Y)]≥𝔼⁡[s⁡(πH,Y)]\mathbb{E}[s(q(H),Y)]\geq\mathbb{E}[s(\pi_{H},Y)]. Choosing q⁡(H)=πHq(H)=\pi_{H} shows that V⁡(H,s)=𝔼⁡[s⁡(πH,Y)]V(H;s)=\mathbb{E}[s(\pi_{H},Y)]. The same argument with MM in place of HH gives V⁡(M,s)=𝔼⁡[s⁡(πM,Y)]V(M;s)=\mathbb{E}[s(\pi_{M},Y)].

It remains to compute the difference V⁡(M,s)−V⁡(H,s)V(M;s)-V(H;s). Since M=μ⁡(H,ζ)M=\mu(H,\zeta) with ζ⟂⟂Y|H\zeta\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid H, Lemma 3 gives ℙ⁡(Y=y∣H,M)=πH​(y)\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid H,M)=\pi_{H}(y) a.s. for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. Then, conditional on (H,M)(H,M),

𝔼[s(πM,Y)−s(πH,Y)∣H,M]=∑y∈𝒴πH(y)(s(πM,y)−s(πH,y))=Ds(πH,πM).\mathbb{E}[s(\pi_{M},Y)-s(\pi_{H},Y)\mid H,M]=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{H}(y)\bigl(s(\pi_{M},y)-s(\pi_{H},y)\bigr)=D_{s}(\pi_{H},\pi_{M}).

Taking expectations gives V⁡(M,s)−V⁡(H,s)=𝔼⁡[Ds​(πH,πM)]V(M;s)-V(H;s)=\mathbb{E}[D_{s}(\pi_{H},\pi_{M})]. Propriety implies Ds​(p,q)≥0D_{s}(p,q)\geq 0 for every p,qp,q, so the right-hand side is nonnegative. If ss is strictly proper, then Ds​(p,q)=0D_{s}(p,q)=0 if and only if p=qp=q, so the gap vanishes if and only if πH=πM\pi_{H}=\pi_{M} a.s. □\square

Theorem 8 shows that, under proper scoring rules, the cost of communication is exactly the amount by which communication distorts the posterior used for the final decision. The next examples show how this gap reduces to familiar quantities under common scoring rules.

Logarithmic loss.

For log loss slog​(q,y)=−log⁡q⁡(y)s_{\log}(q,y)=-\log q(y), interpreted as +∞+\infty when q⁡(y)=0q(y)=0,

V⁡(M,slog)−V⁡(H,slog)=I⁡(Y;H∣M).V(M;s_{\log})-V(H;s_{\log})=I(Y;H\mid M).

Then, if H=BH=B in the common-evidence regime, the exact communication loss is

V⁡(M,slog)−V⁡(B,slog)=I⁡(Y;B∣M).V(M;s_{\log})-V(B;s_{\log})=I(Y;B\mid M).

Under log loss, the pointwise divergence is the Kullback–Leibler divergence, so Dslog(p,q)=KL(p∥q)D_{s_{\log}}(p,q)=\mathrm{KL}(p\|q). Theorem 8 therefore gives

V(M;slog)−V(H;slog)=𝔼[KL(πH∥πM)].V(M;s_{\log})-V(H;s_{\log})=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{H}\|\pi_{M})].

By Lemma 3, ℙ⁡(Y=y∣H,M)=πH​(y)\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid H,M)=\pi_{H}(y) and ℙ⁡(Y=y∣M)=πM​(y)\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid M)=\pi_{M}(y) a.s., so

I(Y;H∣M)=𝔼[∑y∈𝒴ℙ(Y=y∣H,M)logℙ⁡(Y=y∣H,M)ℙ⁡(Y=y∣M)]=𝔼[KL(πH∥πM)].I(Y;H\mid M)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\mathbb{P}(Y{=}y\mid H,M)\log\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y{=}y\mid H,M)}{\mathbb{P}(Y{=}y\mid M)}\right]=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{H}\|\pi_{M})].

Brier score.

For the multiclass Brier score

sBr(q,y)=∑y′∈𝒴(q(y′)−𝟏{y′=y})2,s_{\mathrm{Br}}(q,y)=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\bigl(q(y^{\prime})-\mathbf{1}\{y^{\prime}=y\}\bigr)^{2},
V⁡(M,sBr)−V⁡(H,sBr)=𝔼​‖πH−πM‖22.V(M;s_{\mathrm{Br}})-V(H;s_{\mathrm{Br}})=\mathbb{E}\|\pi_{H}-\pi_{M}\|_{2}^{2}.

Indeed, ∑yp⁡(y)​sBr​(q,y)=1−2​⟨p,q⟩+‖q‖22\sum_{y}p(y)s_{\mathrm{Br}}(q,y)=1-2\langle p,q\rangle+\|q\|_{2}^{2}. Subtracting the same expression at q=pq=p gives DsBr​(p,q)=‖p−q‖22D_{s_{\mathrm{Br}}}(p,q)=\|p-q\|_{2}^{2}. Applying Theorem 8 leads to the claim.

Serial communication under logarithmic loss.

Let M0=HM_{0}=H and suppose

Y→M0→M1→⋯→MLY\to M_{0}\to M_{1}\to\cdots\to M_{L}

is a serial communication chain. Then

V⁡(ML,slog)−V⁡(M0,slog)=∑ℓ=1LI⁡(Y;Mℓ−1∣Mℓ).V(M_{L};s_{\log})-V(M_{0};s_{\log})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}I(Y;M_{\ell-1}\mid M_{\ell}).

Thus each communication stage contributes a nonnegative term under log loss, and the total communication loss on a serial path is additive. To see this, fix k∈{1,…,L}k\in\{1,\dots,L\}. Since Y→Mk−1→MkY\to M_{k-1}\to M_{k} is Markov and the spaces are standard Borel, the kernel from Mk−1M_{k-1} to MkM_{k} admits a universal-randomization representation. There exist ancillary randomness ζk\zeta_{k} with ζk⟂⟂Y|Mk−1\zeta_{k}\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid M_{k-1} and a measurable map μk\mu_{k} such that Mk=μk​(Mk−1,ζk)M_{k}=\mu_{k}(M_{k-1},\zeta_{k}) (Bertsekas and Shreve 1978, Kallenberg 2002, see, e.g.,). The log-loss identity above then applies to each pair (Mk−1,Mk)(M_{k-1},M_{k}), giving

V⁡(Mk,slog)−V⁡(Mk−1,slog)=I⁡(Y;Mk−1∣Mk).V(M_{k};s_{\log})-V(M_{k-1};s_{\log})=I(Y;M_{k-1}\mid M_{k}).

Summing from k=1k=1 to LL gives the result.

Remark 4.

In many empirical studies for LLM-based multi-agent planning, communication is assessed through coarse proxies such as transcript length, number of roles, or number of rounds. Theorem 8 shows that these proxies are not the relevant object for reliability. The relevant object is the posterior distortion. Two systems with the same number of stages can have very different communication loss if one preserves the decision-relevant posterior and the other does not. Likewise, a longer multi-stage system need not be worse if the extra stage preserves the posterior, while a short system can still be highly destructive if it compresses the shared signal poorly. Accordingly, when architectures are compared under the same exogenous information, the right question is not whether one system communicates more, but whether its communication preserves the information needed for the terminal decision. Under proper scoring rules, Theorem 8 gives an exact way to state this comparison. It therefore suggests a more informative evaluation criterion for agent systems. One should measure reliability loss at the level of posterior distortion induced by communication, rather than infer it from organizational complexity alone.

6 Signal Acquisition and Human Review

This section studies two ways to improve reliability once the terminal information state is given. One is to add a new exogenous signal, which can improve the decision problem if it contributes non-redundant information. The other is to add a human review option, which changes the available action at the terminal stage. These two interventions serve different purposes. New signals improve the information available for the final decision, while review changes how the system responds when uncertainty remains. The next corollary studies the value of added signals, and the theorem after that characterizes the optimal selective review.

Corollary 9.

Let MM be the terminal information state of an automated information structure. If an additional verifier signal WW is available at the terminal stage, then for every bounded loss ℓ\ell, V⁡((M,W),ℓ)≤V⁡(M,ℓ)V((M,W);\ell)\leq V(M;\ell), with strict inequality for some bounded loss whenever (M,W)(M,W) is not Blackwell-dominated by MM as an experiment about YY (that is, whenever the additional signal WW is not redundant given MM for the purpose of predicting YY). In particular, self-critique that only re-reads MM cannot move the Bayes envelope, but executable tests or external validators can.

Proof. Any MM-measurable decision rule is also (M,W)(M,W)-measurable, so the infimum over (M,W)(M,W)-measurable rules can only be smaller, i.e., V⁡((M,W),ℓ)≤V⁡(M,ℓ)V((M,W);\ell)\leq V(M;\ell) for every bounded loss ℓ\ell. If WW is Blackwell-redundant relative to MM for YY, meaning that (M,W)(M,W) is generated from MM through a conditionally independent kernel as an experiment about YY, then Lemma 4(a) implies equality for every bounded loss. Conversely, if WW is not Blackwell-redundant, then (M,W)(M,W) is not Blackwell-dominated by MM, and Lemma 4(b) yields a bounded loss ℓ~\tilde{\ell} with V⁡((M,W),ℓ~)<V⁡(M,ℓ~)V((M,W);\tilde{\ell})<V(M;\tilde{\ell}) (applying the Blackwell-Sherman-Stein comparison theorem (Blackwell 1953, Torgersen 1991)). □\square

Corollary 9 gives the decision-theoretic meaning of verification at the terminal stage, such as a verifier signal, an executable test, or an external check. Its function is to distinguish two cases that are often grouped together in practice. If verification only reprocesses the terminal state, then it does not change the decision problem. If it adds a further signal at the terminal stage, then it changes the information available for the final action and may improve the Bayes value. This separation is useful for the next result, which studies review as a different intervention. Review does not refine the information state itself. Instead, it changes the set of feasible responses once the terminal information state has already been formed.

Theorem 10.

Consider a review-capable terminal stage with information HH. Let Ra​(H):=infa∈𝒜𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(a,Y)∣H]R_{a}(H):=\inf_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(a,Y)\mid H] be the minimum automated posterior risk, and let escalation (to human review) incur a measurable conditional loss Rh​(H)R_{h}(H) with 𝔼​[Rh​(H)]<∞\mathbb{E}[R_{h}(H)]<\infty. Then the optimal value is

infδ𝔼⁡[loss under ​δ]=𝔼⁡[min⁡{Ra​(H),Rh​(H)}].\inf_{\delta}\mathbb{E}[\textnormal{loss under }\delta]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min\{R_{a}(H),R_{h}(H)\}\right].

Moreover, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists an ε\varepsilon-optimal threshold policy that automates on {Ra(H)≤Rh(H)}\{R_{a}(H)\leq R_{h}(H)\} and escalates on {Ra(H)>Rh(H)}\{R_{a}(H)>R_{h}(H)\}. If the automated infimum Ra​(H)R_{a}(H) is attained by an HH-measurable Bayes act a∗​(H)a^{*}(H), then an exact Bayes-optimal decision rule is

δ∗​(H)={a∗​(H),if ​Ra​(H)≤Rh​(H),△,if ​Ra​(H)>Rh​(H).\delta^{*}(H)=\begin{cases}a^{*}(H),&\text{if }R_{a}(H)\leq R_{h}(H),\\[4.0pt] \triangle,&\text{if }R_{a}(H)>R_{h}(H).\end{cases}

Proof. The lower bound and the ε\varepsilon-optimal threshold construction follow from Lemma 5. At each realization H=hH=h, the decision is a pointwise comparison between the automated posterior risk Ra​(h)R_{a}(h) and the review loss Rh​(h)R_{h}(h). Since expected loss is linear in the choice between automate and escalate, the optimal rule selects the smaller quantity pointwise. □\square

Theorem 10 shows that selective review is not a heuristic but a posterior-risk comparison rule. It also clarifies how review relates to the earlier analysis of communication. Communication determines the information state HH at the terminal stage, and the theorem characterizes the best use of review given that state. In this sense, communication and review address different parts of the design problem. Better communication lowers Ra​(H)R_{a}(H) by preserving decision-relevant information. Review matters for the cases in which Ra​(H)R_{a}(H) still exceeds the review loss.

Remark 5.

According to Theorem 10, review should not be triggered by fixed stage counts, by the presence of disagreement alone, or by a blanket rule that sends all difficult tasks to a human after several rounds of internal discussion. These practices treat review as a property of the workflow. The theorem shows that the relevant object is instead the posterior risk at the terminal information state. A long interaction need not require review if the final state supports a low-risk action, and a short interaction may require review if uncertainty remains high. Thus the right review signal is decision quality conditional on the available information, not the organizational form that produced that information.

Remark 6.

Summarizing the analysis in Sections 4-6, the design for LLM-based multi-agent planning can be separated into three distinct questions. The first question concerns information acquisition, namely whether the system obtains any additional exogenous signal beyond the shared evidence. The second concerns communication, namely what terminal information state is produced from the available evidence under the chosen interface. The third concerns recourse, namely whether the residual uncertainty at that terminal state is low enough for automation or should instead trigger review. This decomposition is useful because it separates three effects that are often mixed together in practice. It also makes clear which part of a system change should be credited when reliability improves.

7 Numerical Experiments

This section numerically evaluates the theory with controlled LLM experiments. The evaluation uses 200 four-way multiple-choice questions from MMLU (Hendrycks et al. 2021), with the model selecting one answer from {A,B,C,D}\{A,B,C,D\} under nine experimental conditions (denoted as (A), (B2), (B), (B5), (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}), (C), (D), (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}), and (S)). These nine conditions correspond to workflows that differ in one design dimension at a time, namely delegation depth, communication format, or access to external signals. We also include a coarse posterior distortion analysis for the relay settings using model output distributions as a proxy for belief change across stages. This design helps identify which performance changes are associated with deeper delegation, different communication interfaces, or the introduction of new information. Details of the experimental setup are provided in Appendix A.

Table 2 reports the main comparison results for the nine experimental conditions, including the number of evaluated runs NN, the accuracy Acc. (computed as the fraction of runs in which the model’s final answer matches the correct option), and the corresponding confidence interval CI. The first pattern that can be observed concerns delegation under shared information. Relative to the centralized baseline (A), the relay conditions (B2), (B), and (B5) add stages without adding new exogenous signals, and their performance is substantially lower. On gpt-4.1-mini, accuracy falls from 90.7%90.7\% in (A) to 41.2%41.2\% in (B2), 43.5%43.5\% in (B), and 22.5%22.5\% in (B5). On o4-mini, the analogous drop from (A) to (B) is from 89.9%89.9\% to 37.0%37.0\%. This is the clearest pattern in the table and is consistent with Proposition 6 and Theorem 8 that when added stages mainly reprocess the same underlying information, reliability is limited by how well communication preserves decision-relevant content.

The second pattern concerns interface design while holding workflow depth fixed. Comparing (B) with (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}) keeps the three-stage relay structure but changes the message format. Condition (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}), which uses a more structured posterior-style message format, performs better than condition (B), which uses free-form prose, reaching 75.2%75.2\% rather than 58.1%58.1\% at three stages (on 50 questions; see Figure 3). This suggests that the key design object is not only how many stages communicate, but what information the interface preserves for the final decision.

The third pattern concerns added signals. Conditions (C), (D), (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}), and (S) compare settings in which the system may obtain external information beyond the baseline context. Condition (C) (single agent with Wikipedia) reaches 87.2%87.2\%, which is below the centralized baseline, while (D) (Wikipedia + Semantic Scholar) and (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}) (Wikipedia + Wikipedia) both achieve 89.8%89.8\%. On the synthetic task (S), by contrast, tool access raises accuracy from 24.3%24.3\% to 82.7%82.7\%. These comparison results are consistent with Corollary 9 that additional modules help when they add decision-relevant signal, not merely when they enlarge the workflow.

Figures 1-4 further extend the comparisons in Table 2. Figure 1 focuses on delegation depth by comparing (A), (B2), (B), and (B5). On gpt-4.1-mini, accuracy declines from 90.7%90.7\% with one stage to 41.2%41.2\% with two stages, 43.5%43.5\% with three stages, and 22.5%22.5\% with five stages. Although the two-stage and three-stage relays are close in this finite sample, the broader pattern is that longer relay chains do not recover reliability and may instead amplify loss, with the five-stage relay numerically below the 25%25\% chance level for a four-way task.

Figure 2 turns from overall accuracy to a coarse proxy for the mechanism in Theorem 8. It relates per-question KL(πA∥πB)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{A}\|\pi_{B}) to the corresponding accuracy drop. The correlation is r=0.72r=0.72 for condition (B) and r=0.44r=0.44 for condition (B5). The extracted model probabilities are only proxies for the formal posteriors in the theorem, so the plot should be interpreted qualitatively. Even so, the direction is informative. Questions with larger relay distortion also tend to show larger performance losses, which supports the view that communication quality matters through its effect on the belief state used for the final decision.

Figure 3 compares (B) with (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}). The workflow is held fixed at three stages, so the difference comes from the message format rather than from the number of relays. The posterior relay degrades at about 2.82.8 points per stage, while the prose relay degrades at about 8.58.5 points per stage. At three stages, (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}) reaches 75.2%75.2\% accuracy compared with 58.1%58.1\% for (B). This shows that communication loss depends not only on the number of stages but also on the interface, with a more structured relay preserving more decision-relevant information.

Figure 4 examines conditions (C), (D), (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}), and (S). In Table 2, condition (C) achieves 87.2%87.2\%, which does not improve on the 90.7%90.7\% baseline in (A), suggesting that Wikipedia search is largely redundant in this setting. By contrast, on the synthetic task in condition (S), accuracy rises from 24.3%24.3\% without the tool to 82.7%82.7\% with tool access. This pattern is consistent with Corollary 9, which predicts gains when an added signal contributes genuinely new information.

8 Conclusion

This note develops a decision-theoretic framework for LLM-based multi-agent planning. We represent a multi-agent system as a finite acyclic delegated decision network with exogenous signals, endogenous communication, and optional review. This framework allows us to relate architecture design to information structure, to characterize the common-evidence regime as a budget-constrained signal-design problem, and to express the effect of communication under proper scoring rules as an expected posterior-distortion divergence. We also incorporate signal acquisition and human review into the analysis and illustrate the resulting statics through controlled LLM experiments.

Our analysis suggests a useful way to study LLM-based agent systems in operations research. These systems can be treated not only as computational workflows but as delegated decision mechanisms whose performance is governed by what information enters the system, how that information is transformed across stages, and what is ultimately made available at the point of choice. This perspective helps separate organizational appearance from decision-relevant content and places the evaluation of agent architectures within the framework of Bayes risk, experiment comparison, and information design. In this way, the research can provide a solid foundation for future work on communication-constrained planning, tool-mediated decision support, and human-AI systems with structured recourse.

Appendix A Experiment Details

This appendix provides details for the experiments in Section 7.

A.1 Experimental Setup

We use 200 four-way multiple-choice questions from MMLU (Hendrycks et al. 2021)that are balanced between STEM, Humanities, Social Sciences, and Other. Two OpenAI models are used in the experiments: gpt-4.1-mini, which provides token log-probabilities, and o4-mini, a reasoning model without log-probability access. Although MMLU itself is not a planning benchmark, it provides a controlled setting for studying multi-stage LLM workflows and the information passed to the final decision.

Table 3 summarizes the nine conditions. Conditions (A), (B), (C), (D), and (S) use 30 runs per question. Conditions (B2), (B5), (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}), and (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}) use 10 runs per question. All prompts require a single answer from {A,B,C,D}\{A,B,C,D\}.

In the relay conditions, downstream stages see only the relayed message and not the original question. This restriction is important because in this way, any change in performance then comes from the information passed through the workflow rather than from repeated direct access to the source problem. Total API cost is approximately $70 for the original conditions and $15-25 for the additional conditions.

The nine conditions fall into four groups.

Centralized baseline. Condition (A) is the single-agent baseline. The model sees the question directly and outputs one answer.

Delegation depth under shared evidence. Conditions (B2), (B), and (B5) are serial prose relays of different lengths. They add intermediate stages without adding new external signals. These conditions study how performance changes when the final decision depends on a relayed message rather than on the original question.

Communication format. Condition (Bpost{}_{\text{post}}) uses the same three-stage workflow as (B), but replaces free-text relay with a four-class posterior vector. This condition keeps the workflow fixed and changes only the communication format.

Signal acquisition. Conditions (C), (D), (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}), and (S) examine the role of added signals. Condition (C) gives a single agent access to Wikipedia. Condition (D) uses two specialists with different tools, one with Wikipedia and one with Semantic Scholar, and an aggregator combines their outputs. Condition (Dsame{}_{\text{same}}) uses two Wikipedia specialists, so the number of agents increases but the external source does not become more diverse. Condition (S) is a separate synthetic knowledge-base task with 200 fictional entities whose answers are available only through tool lookup. Its role is different from the MMLU conditions. It is included to provide a setting in which tool access is clearly needed for the final decision and not already contained in the model’s parametric knowledge. It should therefore be read as a mechanism check for added external information rather than as a direct benchmark comparison with the MMLU conditions.

Figure 5 shows the information flow for three representative conditions.

A.2 Prompt Templates

The boxes below show representative prompt templates for the main conditions. The remaining conditions use the same structure with the condition-specific changes described above. The centralized baseline in Box A.2 asks the model to answer directly. The relay conditions in Boxes A.2-A.2 progressively restrict what each stage can see. The tool-based conditions in Boxes A.2-A.2 give the agent access to external retrieval.

A.3 Posterior Extraction

For all gpt-4.1-mini conditions, we extract the token log-probabilities for the four answer tokens A, B, C, and D from the final generation step and normalize them with softmax to obtain the four-class distribution π=(πA,πB,πC,πD)\pi=(\pi_{A},\pi_{B},\pi_{C},\pi_{D}).

In the relay conditions (B), (B2), and (B5), we also probe each intermediate stage by appending the follow-up query “If you had to answer now, which letter would you choose?” The log-probabilities from this probe yield the per-stage distributions π0,π1,…,πL\pi_{0},\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{L}. From these distributions we compute the per-handoff KL divergence KL(πk−1∥πk)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{k-1}\|\pi_{k}) and the total distortion KL(πA∥πB,final)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{A}\|\pi_{B,\text{final}}) reported in Section 7. The KL and accuracy scatter in Figure 2 uses the per-question average across 30 runs.

These extracted distributions are not literal Bayesian posteriors in the formal sense of the theory. They are used as an operational proxy for how much the downstream stage’s belief changes relative to direct access to the original question. Since o4-mini does not expose token log-probabilities, this posterior distortion analysis is carried out only for gpt-4.1-mini.
